title: Pear Tallow Balm: What Actually Happened When I Put Beef Fat on My Face
body:
Okay so. I bought beef fat for my face. I know how that sounds. It was a Tuesday night, maybe Wednesday, and I was scrolling on my phone while my cat tried to sit on the keyboard. My skin was just… mad at me. That weird spring dryness where it’s not cold enough for winter cream but everything still feels tight. I saw this thing for a whipped tallow balm. Pear scent. My first thought was, obviously, “you want me to put what on my face?” Like, cooking grease? From a cow? I almost closed the tab. But then I kept reading. Grass-fed beef tallow, made in France, whipped into a balm. It said it was good for fine lines and winter damage. My knuckles were cracked from all the hand-washing. I was desperate. And curious. So I clicked buy. The whole thing felt ridiculous.

Anyway my coffee is getting cold. The point is, the jar showed up maybe two weeks later. Small glass jar, simple label. It sat on my counter for like three days because I was nervous to open it. I was picturing… I don’t know. Bacon grease. Lard. Something my grandma would have in a tin.

## How I Ended Up Smearing Cow Fat on My Skin

So I finally opened it. The texture was weird. Not bad weird. It was whipped, like they said, but thicker than I expected. Like really dense buttercream from a fancy bakery, the kind that’s not too sweet. I poked it. Cold at first. Then it warmed up on my finger real fast. I smelled it. Pear? Sort of. Not like a Jolly Rancher. More like… you know when you walk past the fruit section and you get that light, clean smell? That. It was gentle. Not perfumey. I was relieved.

I put a tiny bit on the back of my hand. It melted. Like, actually vanished. No greasy film. Just… gone. My skin felt soft. Not sticky. Huh.

I started reading about beef tallow skincare benefits because, I mean, I had to know what I was getting into. The science-y stuff, casually: our skin’s natural oil, sebum, has a bunch of fatty acids in it. Grass-fed beef tallow is apparently super similar. So it’s like your skin recognizes it. It absorbs. It doesn’t just sit on top and clog stuff up. It’s not a new idea either—people have been using animal fats on skin forever. My great-grandma probably used something like this. Lanolin, goose fat, all that old-school wisdom. This was just… a nicer version. Whipped. In a jar. With a pear smell.

So that night, I tried it on my face. A tiny scoop. I warmed it between my fingers and just patted it on. It felt… fine. A little rich. I went to bed expecting to wake up a greaseball.

## What This Pear-Smelling Stuff Actually Does

I didn’t. Wake up a greaseball, I mean. My skin felt calm. Like, actually calm. Not thirsty. Not oily. Just… quiet. That was new.

I kept using it. Just at night. On my driest spots—cheeks, elbows, these cracks on my thumbs that wouldn’t heal. The whipped tallow balm just sank in. It’s hard to describe. It’s not like a lotion that you can feel. It’s more like your skin just drinks it and then forgets about it. But you can tell it’s working because the tightness goes away.

Oh, and my lips. I forgot to mention. I used it on my lips one night when I couldn’t find my chapstick. Game changer. It’s not waxy. It just heals them. Overnight.

The pear scent is subtle. It doesn’t stick around. You smell it when you open the jar and that’s it. It’s fresh. Not fruity in a candy way. It’s nice. Makes the whole “beef fat” thing feel a lot less… agricultural.

I got distracted. My neighbor started mowing his lawn. At 8 AM on a Saturday. Rude.

Where was I. Right, the natural ingredients thing. It’s pretty much just the tallow and some pear oil for scent. That’s it. No list of twenty chemical names I can’t pronounce. I like that. It feels simple. Like you know what you’re putting on you.

## My Skin After a Few Weeks of This Experiment

So it’s been maybe a month now. Maybe six weeks. I lost track. I’m bad with time.

But my skin is different. The spring dryness never really hit. My elbows are smooth. I didn’t even know elbows could be a thing I thought about, but here we are. They’re smooth. The cracks on my hands are gone. My face just looks… healthier? Not “glowing” in that weird Instagram way. Just not irritated. Even-keeled. I used to have this dry patch on my cheek that would flake with foundation. It’s just gone now. I didn’t do anything else different.

I told my mom about it. She was horrified at first. “Beef tallow? On your *face*?” Then I let her try it. She stole my jar for her knuckles. Now she wants one. I got mine from this little Etsy shop, just a person making small batches. It feels good to buy from someone like that, not a big factory.

I’m on my second jar now. I use it every night. Sometimes in the morning if it’s really dry out. It’s become my thing. My partner even uses it on his beard when it gets scraggly. Works for that too.

It’s weird how something that sounds so bizarre actually makes so much sense. Your skin knows what to do with it. All those fancy bottles I had before, with the fancy prices… this simple jar of whipped tallow works better. Go figure.

## Would I Buy This Pear Tallow Balm Again?

Yeah. I already did.

It just works. I don’t know what else to say. It’s not magic. It’s not going to make you look 20 again. But if your skin is dry, or irritated, or just being difficult for no reason… this calms it down. It feels like a secret. A really old, simple secret that got packaged nicely and smells like spring pears.

Anyway. If you’re curious about tallow skincare, might be worth a shot. Start with your hands or elbows if you’re nervous. That’s what I did. My skin’s happy. I’m happy. That’s all I wanted.

---

## Quick Questions I Get Asked

**Is beef tallow good for your face?**
Yeah, surprisingly. Because it’s so similar to our skin’s own oils, it absorbs really well. It doesn’t just sit there. It’s like giving your skin something it already knows how to use.

**Does tallow balm clog pores?**
Not in my experience. And from what I read, because it’s so similar to sebum, it actually helps balance things out. It absorbs deep instead of clogging the surface. My skin feels clearer, if anything.

**What does the pear tallow balm smell like?**
It’s light. Fresh. Like the smell of a pear, but not sugary. It’s not strong at all—you really only smell it when you open the jar. Then it fades. It’s just a nice, gentle touch.
